strengths: Proposes a clear and useful architectural idea: decoupling target-position guidance from content representations via query/key-value separation, enabling random-order autoregressive image generation with batched queries and KV-cache reuse.

Empirical results on ImageNet 256x256 are strong on the efficiency-quality tradeoff: ARPG achieves competitive FID while substantially improving throughput and memory over raster AR and random-order AR baselines such as LlamaGen, PAR, and RandAR.
The paper includes relevant ablations on decoder design, shared KV, number of sampling steps, and generation order, which support several core design choices.

The method is practically appealing because the same random-order mechanism naturally supports inpainting, outpainting, resolution expansion, and controllable generation with limited architectural changes.
weaknesses: The theoretical framing overstates the method as autoregressive parallel decoding. Generating multiple tokens in one step assumes conditional independence among those targets given the existing KV cache, so it is not an exact factorization of the fully autoregressive joint distribution; this approximation is not analyzed rigorously.

Novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental relative to RAR, RandAR, PAR, and masked/parallel visual generation. The main advance is an efficient implementation of positional guidance with cross-attention-style queries, rather than a fundamentally new generative principle.

Evaluation of zero-shot generalization is mostly qualitative. Inpainting, outpainting, editing, and resolution expansion are central claims, but the paper lacks quantitative comparisons, user studies, or task-specific metrics against suitable baselines.

Some comparisons are not fully satisfying: efficiency excludes tokenizer cost, controllable generation uses a limited baseline set and even estimates ControlVAR FID from histograms, and the 512x512 result is only a fine-tuned XL model whose FID is not competitive with the best reported methods.
The best generation quality is not state of the art: ARPG-XXL FID 1.94 trails RAR-XL and MAR-L on ImageNet 256x256, so the contribution is mainly efficiency rather than overall sample quality.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a large-scale generative model: code, pretrained models, exact sampling schedules, training compute, and baseline timing methodology are not clearly provided in the manuscript.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence, especially statements about robust zero-shot generalization and setting new benchmarks for quality and efficiency. The evidence supports a strong efficiency-quality tradeoff, but not all broader claims.

strengths: Addresses an important problem in visual autoregressive generation: improving inference efficiency while retaining random-order flexibility for tasks such as inpainting and outpainting.
The guided-decoding formulation is intuitive and provides a clean way to separate content tokens from target-position queries, making the connection to randomized decoding easy to follow.
Empirical results show strong throughput and memory advantages over several autoregressive baselines, especially compared with raster-order LlamaGen and RandAR-style random-order models.
The paper includes useful ablations on decoder allocation, shared KV caching, generation steps, and generation order.
The method appears practically useful for ImageNet class-conditional generation and can be adapted to controllable generation with relatively small architectural changes.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat limited. The work is very close in spirit to RAR, RandAR, MaskGIT-style masked generation, and encoder-decoder/cross-attention formulations with learned queries. The paper does not convincingly establish that the proposed guided decoder is a fundamentally new paradigm rather than an efficient recombination of known ideas.

The central parallel-decoding claim is under-justified. The paper states that multiple target tokens can be predicted independently, but this changes the exact autoregressive factorization because tokens generated in the same block cannot condition on each other. The implications of this approximation are not analyzed theoretically or empirically beyond FID/throughput curves.

Some technical presentation is shaky. For example, the causal mask definition around Eq. 11 appears inconsistent with standard causal attention indexing, and the proof about unmasked-token queries is narrow and does not strongly justify the broader architectural claims.

The empirical claims are overstated. ARPG is not clearly superior in sample quality: RAR and MAR report better FID in key 256x256 comparisons, and the 512x512 result is worse than DiT and VAR in FID. The main advantage is efficiency, not overall generation quality, but the prose repeatedly suggests state-of-the-art or superior quality.

Efficiency comparisons may not be fully fair or reproducible. The paper reports throughput/memory for many external methods under a specific setup, excludes tokenizer cost, and does not give enough detail to verify whether all models were equally optimized, run with comparable kernels/caches, and evaluated under matched quality-compute tradeoffs.

The controllable-generation evaluation is thin. The gains over ControlAR are very small, one baseline is estimated from histograms, and only ImageNet Canny/depth results are reported. This is insufficient to support broad claims about controllable generation.

The zero-shot generalization section is almost entirely qualitative. Inpainting, outpainting, editing, and resolution expansion are presented through examples without quantitative metrics, baselines, human studies, or failure analysis.

Ablations do not isolate several important design choices: target-aware query construction, random-order training versus blockwise decoding, RoPE extrapolation effects, schedule choice, CFG scale tuning, and the role of the two-pass architecture relative to a standard cross-attention decoder.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper provides pseudocode, but key details such as training compute, data preprocessing, exact sampling schedules, code availability, random seeds, and statistical variability are missing or underdeveloped.

Overall, this is a technically plausible and potentially useful efficiency paper, but the evidence and positioning fall below what I would expect for acceptance at a top-tier AI conference. The method’s practical speedups are real strengths, yet the novelty, rigor, and breadth of evaluation are not strong enough to clear the bar.

strengths: Clear and timely contribution: the paper proposes a guided-decoding autoregressive image model that supports random-order generation while retaining causal attention and KV-cache efficiency.

The method is technically well motivated and cleanly positioned against raster AR, masked modeling, RAR, RandAR, PAR, and VAR-style approaches. The decoupling of positional guidance as queries from content as key/value states is an elegant design.

Empirical results on ImageNet 256x256 are strong: ARPG achieves competitive or better FID than many recent AR baselines while offering substantially higher throughput and much lower memory use, especially compared with RandAR and raster-order AR models.
The evaluation includes useful ablations on decoder design, shared KV cache, sampling steps, and generation order, which support the main efficiency-quality claims.
The paper demonstrates broader utility beyond class-conditional generation, including controllable generation and qualitative zero-shot inpainting, outpainting, editing, and resolution expansion.
The presentation is generally clear, with helpful diagrams and pseudo-code in the supplement.
weaknesses: The zero-shot generalization claims are supported mostly by qualitative examples. Quantitative inpainting/outpainting/editing evaluations would make this part much more convincing.

The controllable-generation comparison is somewhat limited: one key baseline's FID is estimated from histograms, and the evaluation is restricted to ImageNet-style canny/depth conditioning rather than broader control benchmarks.

The 512x512 results are less compelling than the 256x256 results: ARPG is much faster, but its FID is worse than DiT-XL/2 and VAR-d36, so the high-resolution quality claim should be stated more carefully.

The theoretical justification relies on assumptions such as independence among simultaneously predicted tokens during parallel decoding; the paper would benefit from a sharper discussion of approximation error and when parallel blocks may degrade consistency.

Efficiency comparisons are useful but not fully standardized: they exclude tokenizer execution and depend on batch size/hardware choices, so the reported speedups may not directly translate to all deployment settings.
Reproducibility details are decent but incomplete for a large-scale generative paper: compute budget, random seeds, training stability, and release plans are not clearly specified.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful architectural idea: decoupling content representation from position-guided prediction via a two-pass decoder, enabling random-order autoregressive image generation with parallel queries and KV caching.

The main ImageNet-1K 256x256 results are strong: ARPG reports competitive or better FID than several recent AR and parallel AR baselines while substantially improving throughput and memory at comparable parameter scales.

The method is well motivated relative to raster-order AR, MaskGIT-style bidirectional masked models, VAR/blockwise AR, and RandAR; the paper explains why positional guidance and separation of query/KV streams matter.

The experimental section includes multiple model scales, 256x256 and 512x512 settings, speed/memory profiling, and useful ablations on decoding steps, attention pattern, architecture split, KV sharing, and positional encoding.
The appendix provides implementation hyperparameters and PyTorch-style pseudocode, which improves reproducibility compared with many image-generation submissions.
weaknesses: Several broader claims are under-supported. Zero-shot inpainting, outpainting, resolution expansion, and editing are evaluated mostly qualitatively, without quantitative comparisons to task-specific or zero-shot baselines.

The text-to-image evaluation is limited: it uses selected GenEval metrics, a small 4M-data setting, and relatively narrow comparisons. The reported overall score is not clearly stronger than LlamaGen and is below SD-v1.5, so the text-to-image claims should be framed more modestly.

Efficiency comparisons may not be fully apples-to-apples: profiling considers only token generation on a single A800 setup, and it is unclear whether tokenizer/decoder overhead, preprocessing, and end-to-end latency are included consistently across methods.

The inference-time shift from causal training to block-wise/local bidirectional attention is empirically useful but theoretically somewhat hand-waved; the claim that it does not compromise the probabilistic model needs a more rigorous treatment.
The paper relies heavily on FID/IS/precision/recall for image quality. There is no human evaluation, diversity/stability analysis across seeds, or uncertainty around reported metrics.

Reproducibility remains incomplete without released code, pretrained checkpoints, exact data subset construction for text-to-image, and detailed evaluation scripts; the pseudocode and hyperparameters are helpful but not sufficient for full replication.

Some comparisons use results from prior papers with potentially different training budgets, tokenizers, or evaluation implementations, and the paper does not fully disentangle gains from the architecture versus tokenizer/training recipe choices.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: improving the efficiency and flexibility of autoregressive image generation while retaining KV-cache-style inference.
The proposed two-pass architecture is intuitive and technically plausible, separating content representation from position-guided prediction in a way that supports random-order and parallel decoding.

The ImageNet class-conditional results are strong on paper: ARPG reports competitive or better FID than several recent AR and parallel AR baselines while using substantially fewer decoding steps and less memory.
The paper includes useful ablations on decoding steps, attention pattern, architectural allocation between the two passes, shared KV projection, positional encoding, and sampling order.

The method is explored across several settings beyond standard class-conditional generation, including controllable generation, text-to-image generation, inpainting, outpainting, and resolution expansion.
weaknesses: The novelty is not fully convincing. The core idea is closely related to XLNet-style two-stream attention, RandAR-style explicit position conditioning, and masked/parallel decoding, but the paper does not sharply establish what is fundamentally new beyond a particular architectural reconfiguration.

The central theoretical motivation is weak. The argument that masked modeling is inefficient because unmasked queries receive no direct gradient is only a partial observation and does not convincingly imply the proposed architecture is necessary or optimal; shared parameters and indirect gradients make the claim less clean than presented.

A key empirical choice, generalizing causal training to block-wise attention at inference, introduces a train-test mismatch. The paper asserts this does not compromise the probabilistic model, but the justification is largely empirical and the probabilistic interpretation is not rigorously resolved.

The zero-shot generalization claims are under-supported. Inpainting, outpainting, editing, and resolution expansion are shown mostly qualitatively, without quantitative benchmarks, baselines, user studies, or failure analysis.

The text-to-image evaluation is limited and not very compelling: only selected GenEval metrics are reported, the overall score is below Stable Diffusion v1.5 and Chameleon, prompts are mostly omitted in the main paper, and standard evaluations such as COCO FID/CLIP or broader alignment metrics are missing.

Efficiency comparisons may not be fully fair or reproducible. The paper profiles token generation only on one A800 GPU, does not clearly state whether all baselines were reimplemented under identical optimized kernels, and omits end-to-end costs including tokenization, conditioning, and training compute.

Some comparisons are potentially misleading. For controllable generation, adapter parameters are excluded, and for 512x512 generation the model is fine-tuned from 256x256 rather than trained comparably to all baselines.

The strongest claims, such as setting a new benchmark for efficient high-performance AR generation, feel stronger than the evidence because code, checkpoints, statistical variance, and detailed reproduction procedures are not provided.
The paper has clarity and polish issues, including typos, awkward phrasing, inconsistent notation, and occasional overclaiming, which make the technical argument harder to trust.

Overall, the work is technically plausible and has promising empirical results, but the combination of limited novelty, weak theoretical support, qualitative-only generalization evidence, and incomplete fairness/reproducibility details leaves it slightly below the acceptance threshold for a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and meaningful architectural idea: decoupling content representation from position-guided prediction via a two-pass causal/cross-attention decoder. This is a plausible and well-motivated way to support random-order parallel generation while retaining KV-cache efficiency.

The main ImageNet-1K results are strong. ARPG reports competitive or better FID than recent AR and parallel AR baselines while substantially improving throughput and memory, especially compared with LlamaGen, VAR, RandAR, PAR, and NAR at similar scales.

The paper evaluates multiple model scales and resolutions, and includes useful ablations on decoding steps, attention pattern, decoder allocation, KV projection sharing, positional encoding, and sampling order.

The method has attractive practical flexibility: the same framework is demonstrated for class-conditional generation, text-to-image generation, controllable generation, inpainting, outpainting, and resolution expansion.
The paper is generally well written, with clear diagrams and enough implementation detail in the appendix to understand the architecture, training setup, and sampling procedure.
weaknesses: The strongest zero-shot generalization claims are supported mainly by qualitative examples. Inpainting, outpainting, editing, and resolution expansion would be much more convincing with quantitative metrics or comparisons to relevant task-specific and zero-shot baselines.

The comparison protocol raises some fairness and reproducibility questions. Throughput and memory are measured only for token generation on one A800 setup, while many baseline numbers appear to be taken from prior work and may not reflect identical kernels, tokenizers, batching, precision, CFG settings, or engineering optimization.

The text-to-image evaluation is limited. ARPG is faster and trained on less data, but its GenEval overall score is similar to LlamaGen and below SD-v1.5; the paper’s text-to-image claims should therefore be framed more cautiously.

The theoretical justification around block-wise inference and the claim that it does not compromise the probabilistic model are not fully satisfying. The method intentionally changes the attention pattern at inference, and while empirically useful, the formal relationship to the trained causal factorization deserves a more careful treatment.

The method depends on a pretrained discrete tokenizer and inherits its representational limits, but the paper does not analyze sensitivity to tokenizer choice, codebook size, or tokenizer reconstruction quality.

Reproducibility is incomplete without released code, trained checkpoints, detailed baseline remeasurement scripts, and exact evaluation settings for FID/IS/precision/recall and GenEval. The appendix helps, but not enough to fully reproduce the headline efficiency and quality claims.
